summary.text: 干 is an old pictograph interpreted chiefly as a shield, with an early defensive use. The same graph is also used in simplified Chinese for the distinct words written traditionally as 乾 ‘dry’ and 幹 ‘trunk’; those spellings do not establish that the words developed from ‘shield’.

formation.text: Pictographic: the whole graph is interpreted as a shield, rather than as a compound of phonetic and semantic parts. Some proposed Shang forms are disputed; the secure attestation identified in this dossier is a mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a shield, reportedly with feather decoration. This is a pictorial account of the character as a whole, not a decomposition into smaller components. A competing interpretation identifies some oracle-bone forms with 單 and a forked hunting implement.

history.text: The dossier reports proposed Shang forms, but their identification as 干 is disputed. A mid-Western Zhou bronze inscription is given as the secure attestation; later Western Zhou forms regularize the forked top to a short horizontal stroke, which continues in later script traditions. The account describes these shapes but does not provide inspected glyph images here.

The Han-period Shuowen explanation analyzes 干 as 反入 plus 一 and gives the sense ‘offend/violate’. This is a historical analysis of the graph and its meaning, distinct from the shield interpretation; it does not independently confirm the pictorial origin.

uncertainties.text: The shield interpretation has substantial scholarly support, but some proposed Shang signs and distinctions between 干 and 盾 remain disputed. Another proposal treats certain oracle-bone forms as variants of 單 depicting a forked hunting implement. The dossier does not establish the depicted object's ancient name or pronunciation.

The use of 干 for the words written 乾 and 幹 in traditional Chinese is a modern simplified-writing correspondence in this dossier; it does not demonstrate an ancient graphic derivation or semantic development from ‘shield’. The date and precise history of these spelling uses are not established here.

senses.period: Securely attested by the mid-Western Zhou, according to the dossier; earlier Shang attribution is proposed and disputed.
senses.text: The graph is interpreted as a shield pictograph. The dossier reports an early defensive use and bronze examples for ‘shield’; the earliest secure attestation it identifies is mid-Western Zhou.

senses.period: Early textual and inscriptional use reported; exact first date unresolved.
senses.text: A defensive or protective use is reported in an oracle-bone example and in a later bronze inscription. This fits the shield interpretation, though the dossier does not establish a full chronology of the sense.

senses.period: Han-period dictionary explanation; date of the word sense unresolved.
senses.text: Shuowen gives ‘offend/violate’ as a sense and analyzes the graph as 反入 plus 一. This historical dictionary account is separate from the proposed shield origin; the evidence here does not establish how or when this sense arose.

senses.gloss: dry (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 乾)
senses.period: Modern simplified spelling; the onset of the word sense is undated here.
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 is used to write the word traditionally written 乾. The dry sense is attested in the Book of Odes, but the dossier does not establish when the dry reading began or a semantic development from ‘shield’.

senses.gloss: trunk; main stem (written 干 in simplified Chinese; traditionally 幹)
senses.period: Modern simplified spelling; historical examples of 幹 are cited without establishing this spelling's origin.
senses.text: In simplified Chinese, 干 is used to write the word traditionally written 幹. Early textual examples cited for 幹 mean a tree stem or the body's frame; they do not establish that this word developed from the shield sense of 干.

developments.text: Using a shield to defend provides a plausible relation between the object and defensive use, and the dossier reports both. It does not document a precise sequence of semantic change.

limitations.text: The dossier reports the dry and trunk words under 干 in simplified writing and gives traditional graphs 乾 and 幹. It does not establish their chronology as spellings or any semantic transition from the shield word.
The chronology and development of the ‘offend/violate’ sense are not established by the historical dictionary explanation alone.

overview.text: 干 is an old graph interpreted as a shield, with a reported early defensive use. In simplified Chinese it also writes the separate words traditionally spelled 乾 ‘dry’ and 幹 ‘trunk’.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a shield; some early forms are disputed, and the object's ancient name is not established here.

takeaway.text: The simplified spellings 干 for ‘dry’ and ‘trunk’ do not show that those words developed from ‘shield’.
